mainTopic: Rules of private and public fasts: shoes, postponing a fast, dream fasts, and the stages of fasting for rain
overview: The amud opens by finishing the definition of dozing (נמנום) before a fast. רב rules that someone who accepts a private fast may not wear shoes, in case he accepted a תענית צבור. The fix is to say clearly that it is a תענית יחיד. The גמרא then describes how different אמוראים handled shoes, and explains that in בבל only תשעה באב is a full communal fast. Next, רב teaches that a person may 'borrow' a private fast and repay it later, and there are two versions of שמואל's reaction. A story about a guest who would not eat shows that a תענית חלום cannot be postponed: it must be kept on the day of the dream, even on שבת. A new משנה then lays out the growing stages of public fasts when no rain falls, ending with mourning-like behavior and fasting by the יחידים until ניסן ends. The גמרא explains from a פסוק in יואל why work is forbidden on these fasts and why that ban begins in the morning. It ends with אביי's schedule for the fast day.

steps.title: What counts as dozing
steps.stepSummary: Dozing is a half-asleep state: the person answers when called, but cannot give a reasoned reply. He remembers things when reminded.
steps.simpleTranslation: Asleep and not asleep, awake and not awake: when people call him he answers, but he can't give a sensible reply, and when they remind him of something he remembers it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its answer to an earlier question: what exactly is 'dozing' (נמנום)? It describes the in-between state of someone half asleep.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion said that real sleep ends the time a person may eat before a fast, but dozing does not. So the גמרא needs a clear test for dozing. The test is this: he responds when called, but cannot give a thought-out answer, and he recalls things when reminded.

keyTerms.meaning: to give back a reasoned answer

steps.whatToRemember: Dozing is not real sleep. The person answers when called but cannot reason clearly, and he remembers things when reminded.

phrases.english: Asleep and not asleep,
awake and not awake.
That is, when they call him he answers,
but he does not know how to give a reasoned reply,
and when they remind him, he remembers.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִים וְלָא נִים, תִּיר וְלָא תִּיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers a question asked just before this text began: how do we define dozing?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Dozing means being half asleep and half awake. He answers when called but cannot reason, and he remembers when reminded.

steps.title: A private fast forbids wearing shoes
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא, quoting רב, rules that a person who accepts a private fast may not wear shoes, because he might have accepted a תענית צבור.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said in the name of רב: A person who took a fast upon himself may not wear shoes. We worry that maybe he took on a communal fast.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רב rules that even a private faster may not wear shoes, and gives the reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Shoes are not forbidden on a normal private fast. They are forbidden on a strict תענית צבור. רב worries that the person's words of acceptance were unclear, so he may actually have taken on the stricter communal kind of fast. To be safe, he must keep the shoe prohibition.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling drives everything that follows: how to avoid the problem, the challenge to it, and the different practices of the אמוראים.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said that Rav said:
An individual who took a fast upon himself
is forbidden to wear shoes.
We are concerned that perhaps
he took a communal fast upon himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the definition of dozing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A private faster may not wear shoes, in case he accepted a communal-style fast.

steps.title: How can he avoid the problem?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what a person should do so that this concern does not apply to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: How should he act?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a short setup question. The גמרא asks for a practical fix, and the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's worry is about unclear wording. So the question is really: what wording makes it obvious that he means only a private fast?

phrases.english: How should he act?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי לֶיעְבַּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a practical solution to רב's concern.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What can a person do so that he is not suspected of having accepted a communal fast?

steps.title: Say clearly that it is a private fast
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב שילא says the person should state outright: 'Tomorrow I will be before You in a private fast.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב שילא said: Let him say this: 'Tomorrow I will be before You in a private fast.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. When accepting the fast, the person should say clearly that it is a תענית יחיד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The concern came from vague wording. Saying 'private fast' out loud removes the doubt, so the shoe prohibition no longer applies.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב שֵׁילָא, לֵימָא הָכִי:
phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Sheila said: Let him say this:
Tomorrow I will be before You
in a private fast.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר רַב שֵׁילָא, לֵימָא הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the practical question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: State explicitly that the fast is a private fast.

steps.title: But we see scholars wearing shoes on a fast day
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן tell רב ששת they have seen scholars wear shoes on their way to the fast-day gathering. This suggests shoes are not a concern.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis said to רב ששת: But we see Rabbis who wear their shoes and come to the fast-day gathering!
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן challenge the shoe prohibition using what they have seen scholars actually do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If scholars wear shoes even on a public fast, then the shoe prohibition seems not to apply. If so, why worry about it on a private fast? The proof comes from behavior, not from a source text.

keyTerms.meaning: the place where people gather on a fast day

phrases.english: The Rabbis said to Rav Sheshet:
But we see Rabbis
who wear their shoes
and come to the fast-day gathering!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא קָא חָזֵינַן רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the shoe prohibition from step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that shoes are forbidden on a fast.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Scholars are seen wearing shoes on a fast day, which suggests the prohibition is not kept.

steps.title: Their behavior proves nothing
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת gets angry and says: if you rely on them, maybe they ate too!
steps.simpleTranslation: He got angry and said to them: Maybe they ate too!
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת rejects the proof. People who are lax about the fast are not a model to learn from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His sharp reply means that not everyone keeps the rules properly. Someone who ignores the shoe rule might ignore eating too. So their behavior cannot show what the law is.

phrases.english: He became angry and said to them:
Perhaps they also ate!
phrases.notes: He's being sarcastic: if you copy what they do, you might as well copy them eating too.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיקְּפַד וַאֲמַר לְהוּ: דִּלְמָא מֵיכַל נָמֵי אֲכוּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the challenge.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof taken from what those scholars do.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Lax people's actions do not show what the law is.

steps.title: Wearing shoes in an unusual way
steps.stepSummary: אביי and רבא wore their shoes upside down, on the upper leather. מרימר and מר זוטרא switched the right and left shoes.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי and רבא wore their shoes on the upper leather. מרימר and מר זוטרא switched the right shoe to the left foot and the left to the right.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports how some אמוראים handled shoes on a fast day. They wore them, but in an awkward, unusual way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wearing shoes in a strange way does not count as normal 'wearing shoes'. So these אמוראים avoided the prohibition while still protecting their feet.

keyTerms.meaning: the upper leather of the shoe

phrases.english: Abaye and Rava
wore their shoes on the upper leather.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets. Either way, they wore the shoe upside down.

phrases.english: Mareimar and Mar Zutra
would switch the right shoe to the left foot
and the left shoe to the right foot.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַבָּיֵי וְרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows how leading אמוראים kept the shoe rule in practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wearing shoes in an unusual way avoids the shoe prohibition.

steps.title: In בבל, only תשעה באב is a full communal fast
steps.stepSummary: The scholars of רב אשי's school wore shoes normally. They followed שמואל, who said the only full תענית צבור in בבל is תשעה באב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis of רב אשי's school went out in their usual way. They held like שמואל, who said: There is no communal fast in בבל except תשעה באב alone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third practice, wearing shoes normally, and explains the reason behind it using שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's worry was that a private faster might have accepted a full communal fast. According to שמואל, in בבל no fast except תשעה באב has the full strict rules. So in בבל that worry does not apply, and shoes are allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: the scholars of רב אשי's school

steps.whatToRemember: רב: a private faster must avoid shoes in case he accepted a communal fast. Some אמוראים wore shoes in an odd way. רב אשי's school wore them normally, because in בבל only תשעה באב is a full תענית צבור.
steps.confusionAlert: שמואל does not mean that בבל never has public fasts. He means none of them has the full strict rules of a communal fast, except תשעה באב.

phrases.english: The Rabbis of the school of Rav Ashi
would go out in their usual way,
holding like what Shmuel said:
There is no communal fast in Babylonia
except the Ninth of Av alone.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָבְרִי כִּי הָא דְּאָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different practice from step 7, based on שמואל.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In בבל, a private faster need not worry that he accepted a full communal fast, so he may wear shoes normally.

steps.title: A person may borrow his fast and repay it
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes רב: someone who accepted a private fast may push it off to another day and make it up.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: A person may borrow his fast and pay it back later.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a rule from רב about private fasts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If someone committed to fast on a certain day but cannot, he may treat the fast like a loan. He skips it today and pays it back on another day.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
A person may borrow his fast and repay.
phrases.notes: He means: skip the fast today and make it up on a different day.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: לֹוֶה אָדָם תַּעֲנִיתוֹ וּפוֹרֵעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about private fasts after the discussion of shoes on fast days.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A private fast may be postponed and made up on another day.

steps.title: שמואל: a fast is not a vow, so no repayment is needed
steps.stepSummary: שמואל objects to the 'repay' part: accepting a fast is just a commitment to suffer that day, not a נדר, so if he can't, he simply doesn't.
steps.simpleTranslation: When I said this before שמואל, he said to me: Did he accept a vow, so that he must pay it? He only took on himself to suffer. If he can, he suffers; if he can't, he doesn't.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל pushes back on רב's rule, saying there is no need to 'repay' at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב treated the fast like a debt that must be paid back. שמואל says it is not a נדר, only a commitment to afflict oneself on that day. If he cannot do it, the obligation just falls away and nothing is owed.

keyTerms.meaning: that there is no way around it

phrases.english: When I said it before Shmuel,
phrases.notes: The speaker is רב יהודה, telling over what happened when he repeated רב's rule.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לִי: וְכִי נֶדֶר קַבֵּל עֲלֵיהּ,
phrases.english: he said to me: Did he then accept a vow upon himself,
that he has no choice but to pay?
He accepted upon himself to cause himself discomfort.
If he is able, he afflicts himself;

phrases.aramaic: אִי לָא מָצֵי — לָא מְצַעַר נַפְשֵׁיהּ.
phrases.english: if he is not able, he does not afflict himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אַמְרִיתַהּ קַמֵּיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל, אָמַר לִי: וְכִי נֶדֶר קַבֵּל עֲלֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the repayment part of רב's rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word ופורע in רב's rule, which assumes a missed fast must be made up.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only a נדר creates a debt that must be paid. A fast is just a commitment to suffer on that day, so if it can't be kept, nothing is owed.

steps.title: Second version: שמואל says repayment is obvious
steps.stepSummary: In another version of the story, שמואל agrees with רב but calls the rule obvious: at worst a fast is like a נדר, and a נדר can be paid later.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: A person may borrow his fast and repay. When I said this before שמואל, he said: That's obvious! Let it be no worse than a vow. Doesn't a vow need to be paid, even if it is pushed to tomorrow or another day?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of the same conversation, where שמואל's reaction is the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here שמואל does not deny repayment; he says it goes without saying. A fast is at least like a נדר, and a נדר that wasn't kept today is still paid on a later day. In the first version, שמואל said a missed fast need not be repaid at all. In this version, he says repayment is obvious.

keyTerms.meaning: let it be no more than

steps.confusionAlert: Both versions quote the same words from רב. What changes is שמואל's reaction: in the first he says no repayment is needed, in the second he says repayment is obvious.

phrases.english: Some say:
Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
A person may borrow his fast and repay.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אַמְרִיתַהּ קַמֵּיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל, אָמַר לִי:
phrases.english: When I said it before Shmuel, he said to me:
It is obvious! Let it be no more than a vow.

phrases.aramaic: נֶדֶר — מִי לָא מָצֵי בָּעֵי לְשַׁלּוֹמֵי
phrases.english: A vow: doesn't he need to pay it,
going on to tomorrow or another day?
phrases.notes: A נדר that wasn't kept today is still owed later, so a fast can be paid back later too.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an opposite version of שמואל's response from step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to this version, a postponed fast is clearly owed later, just like a נדר.

steps.title: A guest refuses a fine meal because he is fasting
steps.stepSummary: רב יהושע בריה דרב אידי visits רב אסי's house; they prepare a special calf, and he says he is fasting.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהושע son of רב אידי came to רב אסי's house. They prepared a choice calf for him and said: Let the Master taste something. He said: I am fasting.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that will test רב's rule about borrowing a fast. This step sets up the scene.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The hosts went to great effort to honor their guest. His refusal sets up their question in the next step: why not just borrow the fast?

keyTerms.meaning: I am sitting in a fast

phrases.english: Rav Yehoshua son of Rav Idi
happened to come to the house of Rav Asi.
They prepared for him a third-born calf,
phrases.notes: Literally 'a third calf.' It means an especially fine, tender calf, served to honor a guest.

phrases.english: They said to him: Let the Master taste something.
He said to them: I am sitting in a fast.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידֵּי אִיקְּלַע לְבֵי רַב אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a story to show how רב's rule works in practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The guest declines food because he is in the middle of a private fast.

steps.title: The hosts ask: why not borrow the fast?
steps.stepSummary: The hosts challenge him with רב's rule: push the fast off and eat with us.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Let the Master borrow the fast and repay it. Doesn't the Master hold like רב, who said a person may borrow his fast and repay?
steps.whatsHappening: The hosts use רב's rule from step 9 to challenge the guest's refusal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a private fast can be postponed, there is no reason to turn down the meal. He could eat now and fast another day.

phrases.english: They said to him: Let the Master borrow and repay;
does the Master not hold of this
that Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
A person may borrow his fast and repay?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלוֹזֵיף מָר וְלִיפְרַע, לָא סָבַר מָר לְהָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the story into a challenge using רב's rule.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since a private fast may be postponed, he could eat now and make up the fast later.

steps.title: A dream fast cannot be borrowed
steps.stepSummary: He answers that his fast is a תענית חלום, which cannot be pushed off.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: It is a fast for a dream.
steps.whatsHappening: The guest answers that his fast is a special kind that the borrowing rule does not cover.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's rule applies to ordinary private fasts. A fast to cancel the effects of a bad dream has to be done on that day, so it cannot be postponed.

keyTerms.meaning: a fast after a bad dream

phrases.english: He said to them: It is a fast for a dream.
phrases.notes: He had a bad dream and was fasting to cancel its bad effects.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: תַּעֲנִית חֲלוֹם הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the hosts' challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: a dream fast is an exception to the borrowing rule.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any private fast can be borrowed and repaid.
steps.terutzMaskana: A תענית חלום is an exception and must be kept on its day.

steps.title: A fast destroys a bad dream like fire burns chaff
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches that fasting is very effective against a bad dream, which explains why the guest would not give up his fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר מחסיא said in the name of רב חמא בר גוריא in the name of רב: A fast is as good for a dream as fire is for chaff.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a teaching from רב that explains why a dream fast is so important.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Chaff burns up instantly in fire, and a fast wipes out a bad dream just as quickly. This is why the guest would not trade his dream fast for a later day.

keyTerms.meaning: chaff, flax waste that burns instantly

phrases.english: And Rabba bar Machseya said

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חָמָא בַּר גּוּרְיָא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: that Rav Chama bar Gurya said that Rav said:
A fast is effective for a dream
like fire for chaff.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר מַחְסֵיָא אָמַר רַב חָמָא בַּר גּוּרְיָא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer that a dream fast is special.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Fasting is extremely effective at cancelling a bad dream.

steps.title: The dream fast works on that same day
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא adds that the fast must be on the very day of the dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: And on that same day.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא adds a condition to רב's teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fast cancels the dream only if it is done on that day. This is exactly why it cannot be borrowed and paid back later.
steps.whyThisMatters: This condition explains the story: a dream fast pushed to another day would lose its power.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said: And on that same day.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: וּבוֹ בַּיּוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows רב's teaching to a fast on the day of the dream.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dream fast works only on the day of the dream.

steps.title: One may fast for a dream even on שבת
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף says a dream fast may be kept even on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יוסף said: Even on שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף adds that a dream fast is so important that it is kept even on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally fasting on שבת is not allowed, since שבת is a day of enjoyment. Because the fast must be on the day of the dream, it is allowed even then.

phrases.english: And Rav Yosef said: And even on Shabbat.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: וַאֲפִילּוּ בְּשַׁבָּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on 'that same day': even when that day is שבת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dream fast may be kept even on שבת.

steps.title: How does he fix fasting on שבת?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what remedy there is for someone who fasted on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is his remedy?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how a person makes up for having fasted on שבת. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the fast was allowed, fasting on שבת takes away from its enjoyment. The question is how he can fix that.

phrases.english: What is his remedy?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי תַּקַּנְתֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on רב יוסף's ruling allowing a fast on שבת.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How one makes up for having fasted on שבת.

steps.title: A second fast to make up for the first
steps.stepSummary: He should fast another day to make up for fasting on שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him sit in a fast for the fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: he should keep another fast on a weekday to make up for fasting on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first fast fixed the dream, but it also took away from שבת. A second fast on a weekday makes up for that.

keyTerms.meaning: let him fast a fast for the fast

steps.whatToRemember: An ordinary private fast can be postponed and made up later. A תענית חלום is an exception: it must be on the day of the dream, even on שבת, and then one fasts again to make up for fasting on שבת.

phrases.english: Let him sit in a fast for the fast.
phrases.notes: He keeps another fast on a weekday to make up for the fast he kept on שבת.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִיתֵּיב תַּעֲנִיתָא לְתַעֲנִיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He fasts again on another day to make up for fasting on שבת.

steps.title: The court adds three stricter fasts
steps.stepSummary: If the first three communal fasts bring no rain, the בית דין decrees three more, with eating stopped from the night before and five activities forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: If those fasts passed and no rain came, the court decrees three more fasts on the community. People may eat and drink only while it is still day. They may not work, bathe, anoint with oil, wear shoes, or have marital relations, and the bathhouses are locked.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It describes the next level of fasting when the first three communal fasts did not bring rain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These fasts are stricter than the first ones in two ways. The fast starts from the night before, so eating must stop while it is still day. Work, bathing, anointing, shoes and marital relations are all forbidden, just as on יום כיפור.

keyTerms.meaning: The rabbinic court that sets the community's fasts
While it is still day, before nightfall

phrases.english: MISHNA: If these passed and they were not answered —
phrases.notes: “These” are the first three communal fasts from the earlier משנה. “Answered” means rain fell.

phrases.english: the court decrees
three other fasts upon the community.
They eat and drink while it is still day,
and they are forbidden to work and to bathe,
and to anoint with oil and to wear shoes,
and to have marital relations,
and they lock the bathhouses.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ עָבְרוּ אֵלּוּ וְלֹא נַעֲנוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the earlier discussion of dream fasts ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After three unanswered communal fasts, the court decrees three more severe fasts that begin the night before and forbid work, bathing, anointing, shoes and marital relations.

steps.title: Seven more fasts, with extra strictness
steps.stepSummary: If there is still no rain, the court adds seven more fasts, making thirteen in total. On these the alarm is sounded and the stores are closed, with limited openings on Monday and Thursday.
steps.simpleTranslation: If those passed and no rain came, the court decrees seven more, making thirteen fasts on the community. These are stricter than the earlier ones: on them the alarm is sounded and the stores are locked. On Monday stores open a little at nightfall, and on Thursday they may open out of respect for שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה climbs to the next level: seven more fasts, stricter than all the ones before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The number thirteen counts all the communal fasts: three, then three, then seven. Two new things are added: sounding an alarm and closing shops. Shops still open a bit on Monday evening so people can buy food to break the fast, and on Thursday so they can prepare for שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally “they tilt”: they open the shops partway
Respect for שבת, here meaning preparing for it

phrases.english: If these passed and they were not answered,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּית דִּין גּוֹזְרִין עֲלֵיהֶן עוֹד שֶׁבַע
phrases.english: the court decrees upon them seven more,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהֵן שְׁלוֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה תַּעֲנִיּוֹת עַל הַצִּבּוּר.
phrases.english: which make thirteen fasts upon the community.
These are more severe than the first ones,
for on these they sound the alarm,
and they lock the stores.
On Monday they open them a little at nightfall,
and on Thursday they are permitted, out of respect for Shabbat.

steps.triggerLanguage: עָבְרוּ אֵלּוּ וְלֹא נַעֲנוּ, בֵּית דִּין גּוֹזְרִין עֲלֵיהֶן עוֹד שֶׁבַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with the next, stricter stage of fasts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Seven more fasts are decreed, making thirteen in all. On them the alarm is sounded and the stores are closed, with a partial opening on Monday evening and full opening on Thursday.

steps.title: The community acts like mourners
steps.stepSummary: If the thirteen fasts bring no rain, no more fasts are decreed. Instead, everyone cuts back on business, building, planting, weddings and greetings.
steps.simpleTranslation: If those passed and no rain came, people cut back on business, building and planting, betrothals and weddings, and greeting one another, like people whom God has rebuked.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה describes the last stage for the whole community. Instead of more fasts, everyone lowers their joy and normal activity.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court stops adding fasts, probably because the public cannot keep fasting forever. Instead, the community behaves like people who know God is displeased with them, and cuts back on happy and ordinary activities.

keyTerms.meaning: Rebuked by God; המקום is a name for God

phrases.english: If these passed and they were not answered,
they cut back on business,
on building and planting,
on betrothals and marriages,
and on greetings between a person and his fellow —
like people who have been rebuked by God.

steps.triggerLanguage: עָבְרוּ אֵלּוּ וְלֹא נַעֲנוּ, מְמַעֲטִין בְּמַשָּׂא וּמַתָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with the stage after the thirteen fasts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After thirteen unanswered fasts, the community cuts back on business, building, planting, weddings and greetings, as people rebuked by God.

steps.title: Individuals fast until ניסן ends
steps.stepSummary: The יחידים keep fasting until the end of ניסן. Rain that falls after ניסן is a sign of a curse, as the פסוק about the wheat harvest shows.
steps.simpleTranslation: The special individuals go back to fasting until ניסן is over. If ניסן ended and then rain fell, it is a sign of a curse, as it says: “Is it not the wheat harvest today?”
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה ends by saying how long the יחידים keep fasting, and why they stop after ניסן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After ניסן, rain no longer helps the crops and can even ruin the harvest. The פסוק shows that rain at harvest time came as a punishment. So there is no point praying for rain past ניסן.

keyTerms.meaning: Special individuals, the Torah scholars mentioned in the earlier משנה
The spring month that ends the rainy season

steps.whatToRemember: The fasts grow step by step: three, three more, then seven more, then mourning-like behavior. The יחידים keep fasting until the end of ניסן, because rain after that is a curse, not a blessing.

phrases.english: The individuals go back and fast
until Nisan ends.
If Nisan has ended and rains fell —
it is a sign of a curse,
as it is said: “Is it not the wheat harvest today?” and so on.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַיְּחִידִים חוֹזְרִין וּמִתְעַנִּין עַד שֶׁיֵּצֵא נִיסָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the משנה with the rule for the יחידים and the time limit of ניסן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The יחידים fast until the end of ניסן, since rain after ניסן is a sign of a curse.

steps.title: Why is work forbidden, if work is not a pleasure?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that bathing, anointing and marital relations are pleasures, so it makes sense to ban them on a fast. But work is a hardship, so why is it forbidden?
steps.simpleTranslation: Granted, all the others involve pleasure: bathing, anointing and marital relations. But work is suffering!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and challenges the משנה's rule that work is forbidden on these fasts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A fast is meant to cause discomfort, so banning pleasures fits. Work is not a pleasure; it is effort and strain. So banning it seems to go against the purpose of a fast.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted, it makes sense (a lead-in to a challenge)

phrases.english: GEMARA: Granted, all of them
have pleasure in them:
bathing, anointing and marital relations,
but work — it is suffering!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא כּוּלְּהוּ, אִית בְּהוּ תַּעֲנוּג
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions one detail of the משנה in step 20: the ban on work.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that work is forbidden on the stricter communal fasts.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The other bans remove pleasures, which fits a fast. Work is a hardship, so there seems to be no reason to forbid it.

steps.title: A fast day is like a יום טוב, so work is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא, quoting רב ירמיה בר אבא, explains from a פסוק in יואל that a fast is called an עצרת. Just as work is forbidden on an עצרת, it is forbidden on a fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of רב ירמיה בר אבא: The פסוק says, “Sanctify a fast, call an assembly, gather the elders.” A fast is like an assembly day. Just as work is forbidden on an assembly day, so too work is forbidden on a fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by bringing a פסוק that puts a fast day in the same group as a יום טוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban on work does not come from the idea of avoiding pleasure. It comes from a comparison in the פסוק: the fast is called an עצרת, and an עצרת is a day when work is forbidden. So the fast takes on that same rule.

keyTerms.meaning: An assembly day, here meaning a יום טוב, when work is forbidden

steps.confusionAlert: Here עצרת does not mean only שבועות. It means a day of gathering, like any יום טוב, when work is forbidden.
steps.whatToRemember: Work is forbidden on a severe public fast not because it is a pleasure, but because the פסוק in יואל compares the fast to an עצרת, when work is forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא,
phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda said that Rav Yirmeya bar Abba said:
The verse says:
“Sanctify a fast, call an assembly,
gather the elders”:
it is like an assembly day.
phrases.notes: The פסוק puts “fast” and “assembly” side by side, so the fast is treated like a day of assembly.

phrases.english: Just as on an assembly day it is forbidden to do work,
so too on a fast it is forbidden to do work.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא, אָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 24 with a פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Scriptural source that gives a different reason for the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The fast's bans were thought to be only about removing pleasure, so a ban on work made no sense.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban on work comes from the פסוק comparing a fast to an עצרת, when work is forbidden.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the fast day's rules come from two sources: removing pleasure, and being treated like a holy day of gathering.

steps.title: Should the work ban start from the night before, like an עצרת?
steps.stepSummary: If a fast is like an עצרת, then work should be forbidden from the evening before, just as it is on an עצרת.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then just as an עצרת begins from the evening, a fast should also begin from the evening!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes the comparison from step 25 further. If a fast is like an עצרת, maybe the ban on work should also start the night before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 25 we learned that work is forbidden on a fast because the פסוק calls a fast an עצרת. But a יום טוב starts at night, so the comparison seems to say the work ban should start at night too. That does not fit the practice, so the comparison needs a limit.

keyTerms.meaning: A day of assembly, like a יום טוב, when work is forbidden
If so (if your comparison is true)

phrases.english: If so, just as an assembly day is from the evening,
so too a fast should also be from the evening!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי, מָה עֲצֶרֶת מֵאוּרְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how far the עצרת comparison from step 25 should go.
steps.kashyaTarget: The comparison of a fast to an עצרת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the comparison is complete, the work ban should start at night like an עצרת. That is not the practice.

steps.title: A fast is like a gathering of elders, which happens by day
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא, quoting רבי ירמיה בר אבא, says the same פסוק compares a fast to a gathering of elders, which takes place by day.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: רבי ירמיה בר אבא himself explained this to me. The פסוק says, 'Gather the elders.' A fast is like a gathering of elders. Just as a gathering of elders is by day, so too a fast is by day.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא answers the challenge. The same פסוק that calls a fast an עצרת also says 'gather the elders,' and that gathering happens in the daytime.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in יואל gives two comparisons. The עצרת comparison teaches that work is forbidden. The 'gather the elders' comparison teaches when it applies: elders gather by day, not at night. So the work ban on a fast starts in the daytime.

keyTerms.meaning: It was explained to me personally

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
To me it was explained
by Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba himself.
The verse says: "Gather the elders,"
phrases.notes: יואל 1:14. It is the same פסוק that called a fast an עצרת.

phrases.english: meaning a fast is like a gathering of elders.
Just as a gathering of elders is by day,
so too a fast is also by day.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא: לְדִידִי מִיפָּרְשָׁא לִי מִינֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 26 by limiting the עצרת comparison with a second comparison from the same פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A second comparison in the same פסוק sets the time limit.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The work ban on a fast, like on an עצרת, would start from the night before.
steps.terutzMaskana: The fast is also like a gathering of elders, which is by day, so the work ban starts in the daytime.

steps.title: Maybe it should start only from noon
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the fast should not start only from noon, if it depends on a gathering by day.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe say it starts from noon?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 27. If the work ban is tied to the elders' gathering, maybe that gathering, and so the work ban, only begins at midday.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'By day' does not tell us exactly when in the day. If the gathering only starts at noon, the work ban might only start then too. The גמרא needs a source that the gathering starts in the morning.

phrases.english: But say it is from noon?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימָא מִטִּיהֲרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the exact starting time implied by step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: The conclusion that the work ban on a fast starts by day
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'By day' could mean from midday, not from morning.

steps.title: The gathering starts in the morning, as רב הונא said
steps.stepSummary: רב שישא בריה דרב אידי says the answer comes from רב הונא, who taught that the public gathering on a fast starts in the morning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שישא the son of רב אידי said: this supports רב הונא, who said: the gathering is from the morning.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שישא answers the noon question. Since רב הונא taught that the fast-day gathering begins in the morning, the ban on work begins in the morning too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fast is tied to the gathering, and רב הונא says the gathering starts in the morning. So the restrictions start from the morning, not from noon. The comparison to the elders' gathering also backs up רב הונא's view.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי:
phrases.english: Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi said:
This supports Rav Huna,
who said: The gathering is from the morning.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שִׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִידִי: מְסַיַּיע לֵיהּ לְרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 28 by showing that the gathering begins in the morning.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings an existing teaching that fixes the gathering's time as morning.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ban on work might begin only at noon.
steps.terutzMaskana: The gathering, and so the ban on work, start from the morning.
steps.whatToRemember: Work is forbidden on a public fast because it is called an עצרת. It starts in the morning, not the night before, because the fast is like a gathering of elders, which happens by day from the morning.

steps.title: What do they do on the fast day?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the public spends the day of a fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do they act?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new practical question, setting up the next step. Now that we know the gathering starts in the morning, what actually happens during the day?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a challenge but a request for information. It follows naturally from the mention of a morning gathering in step 29.

keyTerms.meaning: How do they act? What do they do?

phrases.english: How do they act?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי עָבְדִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the morning gathering of step 29 and asks what that gathering does.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The order of events on a public fast day.

steps.title: אביי's schedule for the fast day
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the first half of the day is spent checking the town's affairs, a quarter on reading the Torah and הפטרה, and the last quarter on prayer, based on a פסוק in נחמיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: From morning until midday we look into the town's affairs. After that, for a quarter of the day we read from the Torah and the הפטרה. After that we pray for mercy. As the פסוק says: 'They stood up in their place and read in the book of the Torah of ה׳ their God for a quarter of the day, and for a quarter they confessed and bowed down to ה׳ their God.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question by giving the schedule of the day. He brings a פסוק from נחמיה to show that the day is split into reading and praying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The daytime is split into four parts. Two quarters, until midday, go to fixing problems in the town. One quarter goes to reading the Torah and הפטרה, and one to confession and prayer. The פסוק in נחמיה names the reading quarter and the confession quarter.

keyTerms.meaning: We look into the affairs of the town
The הפטרה, the reading from the Prophets
We ask for mercy, we pray

steps.whatToRemember: On a public fast, the first half of the day goes to fixing the town's problems. Then a quarter goes to reading the Torah and הפטרה, and the last quarter to prayer and confession, as in נחמיה.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a public fast is not just about not eating. It is a full day of checking what is wrong in the community, learning, and prayer.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
From the morning until the middle of the day
we examine the affairs of the town.
From here on, for a quarter of the day
we read from the Torah and the Prophets.
From here on we ask for mercy,
as it is said: "And they stood up in their place,"
and they read in the book of the Torah of ה׳ their God
for a quarter of the day,
and for a quarter they were confessing
and bowing down to ה׳ their God."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: מִצַּפְרָא עַד פַּלְגָא דְיוֹמָא מְעַיְּינִינַן בְּמִילֵּי דְמָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 30 with a full schedule and a source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Half the day for the town's affairs, a quarter for reading the Torah and הפטרה, and a quarter for prayer and confession.
